correctness.rationale: Each oriented petal lap rotates exactly its d_i nonhub labels and fixes the others. A closed blank walk based at the hub reduces by backtracks to a concatenation of oriented petal laps and their inverses. Their actions commute, have orders d_i, and act freely on the distinct labels, so there are exactly L hub states in each component. For each nonhub location on a petal, reversing the forward segment from the hub assigns its state a unique initial hub state; thus each oriented lap from a hub state gives a path to the next coordinate state with distinct interior states, and the paths exhaust all nonhub states. Each nonhub blank has just two neighbor choices; at the hub the two directions in each petal are the starts or ends of these paths. In particular a triangle supplies two separate paths between the same two core endpoints. This gives NL vertices, LΣm_i edges and cycle rank 1+(r−1)L. The N! complete labelings split into (N−1)!/L components. A spanning tree omits at most one segment per subdivided edge, since two omissions would strand a nonempty interior section. The full paths give a core spanning tree, and conversely the omitted segment of each remaining path can be chosen in m_i ways. This multiplies the weighted core tree sum by ∏m_i^L. Conductances 1/m_i give mode eigenvalues Σ(4/m_i)sin²(πk_i/d_i), with d_i=2 contributing 4/m_i, not 2/m_i; dividing the nonzero eigenvalue product by L gives the stated ordinary tree count. Binomial multiplicities give the all-triangle specialization. A separate literal-graph exploration suppressed each length-graded chain, compared the exact multigraph to the core, and computed both rational Kirchhoff cofactors. It reproduced all five cited tree counts and checked a mixed (3,4,5) rose as well. The algebraic and graph arguments, not the finite checks, prove the theorem for unrestricted petal parameters.
residual_risks: The graph argument uses a pure rose with no extra board vertices or edges. It does not classify arbitrary cactus puzzles, repeated-label puzzles, or directed spanning trees.

originality.rationale: The bound result's distinct contribution is the exact graph of each multi-petal component, including lengths and multiplicity of its paths, and its consequent all-parameter spanning-tree formula. Credit Wilson for the general monodromy/coset method, from which the component count is a short corollary, and Defant–Kravitz for a cut-vertex proposition that already yields the exact count for all-triangle roses. Neither inspected result gives the edge-resolved component nor an equivalent tree census. Weighted matrix-tree enumeration is standard once the particular core is known. This is not a historical priority claim for the component count, the monodromy method, or the enumeration tool.
residual_risks: The historical comparison is bounded to the exact passages and local index inspected. Less visible graph-cover or puzzle literature may have an equivalent multi-petal shape or tree product. Wilson's component-count coverage is affirmative, not an unresolved access issue.

value.rationale: An explicit component graph determines internal routes and cycle structure, not just which labelings are reachable. The result describes a natural family of cut-vertex puzzles with arbitrarily many unequal petals. Tracking the two genuinely different routes on each triangle is essential to the weighted tree count, which yields exact dependence on the whole vector of petal lengths and serves as an exact structural benchmark for puzzle graphs. The utility does not rely on the component count being new or on an unproved practical claim.
residual_risks: The result describes only pure roses and ordinary undirected trees. No algorithmic or empirical performance advantage is established.
